title: The Law That Keeps Living Faces Off Money
hook: A new $1 coin puts a sitting president's face on U.S. currency for only the second time ever. Legal experts say the law was written to prevent exactly that.
key_points: Long-standing U.S. practice and law bar depicting a living person on federal currency — one reason presidents traditionally appear on money only after they've died.

The U.S. Mint's new $1 coin, issued for the nation's 250th anniversary, features a close-up image of President Trump — making him only the second living president ever depicted, after Calvin Coolidge in 1926.
Constitutional law expert Jeremy Paul told NPR the coin is likely illegal under that rule against depicting living people on currency.
The Treasury Department's defense is that the rule doesn't apply to this coin, citing a 2020 law that specifically authorized a special-edition 250th-anniversary coin.

The dispute is a live example of how two federal statutes can point in different directions — a general rule and a specific carve-out — leaving the outcome to depend on which one a court decides controls.
content_html: Ever wonder why U.S. currency almost never shows a sitting president's face? It's not just tradition — federal law and long practice have kept living people, including whoever currently holds office, off the money. A new coin is testing exactly how firm that rule is.
extra_html: Per NPR's Rachel Treisman, the U.S. Mint's new $1 coin for the nation's 250th anniversary features a close-up image of President Trump, making him only the second living president ever depicted on U.S. currency, after Calvin Coolidge appeared on a coin in 1926. Constitutional law expert Jeremy Paul told NPR the coin is likely illegal under the rule against putting a living person's likeness on currency. The Treasury Department disagrees, arguing that rule doesn't govern this particular coin because a 2020 law specifically authorized a special-edition 250th-anniversary design. Both sides have a real statute to point to — a general rule on one hand, a specific carve-out on the other — which is precisely the kind of conflict that, absent a settlement, ultimately needs a court, not just a press statement, to resolve. flashcards.prompt: What long-standing rule does U.S. currency law generally follow regarding presidents' portraits?
flashcards.back_html: Living people, including sitting presidents, generally aren't depicted on federal currency — a rule meant to avoid glorifying current officeholders on money everyone has to use.

flashcards.prompt: Who was the only other living president depicted on U.S. currency before Trump's 2026 coin, per NPR?

choices.text: George Washington, on the original dollar bill
No other living president has ever appeared on U.S. currency

flashcards.explanation_html: NPR reported the new coin makes Trump only the second living president ever depicted on U.S. money, after Coolidge in 1926.

flashcards.prompt: How does the Treasury Department defend issuing a coin that a constitutional law expert says breaks the living-person rule?

choices.text: By citing a separate 2020 law that specifically authorized a special-edition 250th-anniversary coin
By arguing the rule against living persons on currency does not legally exist
By arguing the Supreme Court already approved this specific coin in advance
